qrdBas-de78pp.summary: Bassolis's prologue to Book 1 is eight questions on the possibility, necessity, subject, scientific status, unity, and practical character of theology, built throughout in dialogue with Scotus, Aquinas, and Henry of Ghent. q1 develops a theory of cognition in which intuition differs from abstraction chiefly by immediacy and God can cause intuition of non-existents. On that basis it argues that evident abstractive knowledge of God, and so demonstrative theological science, is possible for a wayfarer by divine power, though intuitive vision is not, and that faith and science are compossible; it closes with a principium sermon on Hosea commending Book 1. q2 argues that revealed doctrine is necessary for man's supernatural end, its means, and God's proper features, while judging all such arguments probable rather than demonstrative and treating revealed knowledge as natural relative to the receiving intellect but supernatural relative to its agent. q3 and q4 establish that the subject of theology is God under the proper ratio of deity, which virtually contains all theological truths and is formally distinct (ex natura rei) from the divine attributes. They reject goodness, relations of reason, the credible, the revealable, the Word, the whole Christ, and Scotus's 'infinite being', give the divine will under its determination a relative primacy for contingent truths, and deny that God is the subject of metaphysics. q5 defines science strictly and concludes that only God's, the blessed's, and a possible revealed abstractive theology are sciences. Our theology is neither subalternate to the science of the blessed (against Aquinas) nor science in an intermediate light (against Henry); it is a 'certain extended faith' of exegetical and deductive habits. q6 holds that formal science is the habit of a single conclusion, so our theology is an aggregate of habits unified by order, distinct from all other sciences and neither subalternating nor subalternate to any. q7 defines praxis as an act of will directable by right reason and argues, against Scotus, that knowledge is practical from appetite for the end, not from its object. q8 applies this: God's and the blessed's theology are speculative because their wills cannot err, while our theology, pursued from love of God to direct charity, is simply practical and the noblest science in via. Beatitude consists principally in love.
claims: Evident abstractive knowledge of God, and demonstrative theology, is possible for a wayfarer by divine power; intuitive vision is not.
Revealed doctrine is necessary for man's supernatural end, though arguments for this are probable rather than demonstrative.
God under the ratio of deity, formally distinct from the attributes, is the subject of theology.
Our theology is not science in the strict sense but a 'certain extended faith', neither subalternate to the blessed's science nor science in an intermediate light.
Our theology is an aggregate of distinct habits unified by order and independent of metaphysics.
Knowledge is practical from appetite for the end, not from its object; our theology is simply practical, while God's and the blessed's is speculative.

qrdBas-de2604.summary: Distinction 37 of Book 1 is treated in a single question on whether God is everywhere. Bassolis affirms, by the authority of Ambrose, Augustine, and Gregory rather than by reason, that God is present by essence, by presence (perfect knowledge), and by power (conservation and governance). He specifies that being everywhere per se, necessarily, as a singular, and without real relation to place is proper to God. His main contribution is a sustained denial that omnipresence can be demonstrated from omnipotence or divine action. Natural agents such as the sun act immediately on distant things, an omnipotent agent acting by will needs no presence to its object, and creation presupposes no presence, so omnipresence by immensity is held by faith alone. Aristotle's contact principle holds only for qualitative corporeal agents, and God's new presence to new creatures involves no change in God.
claims: God is everywhere by essence, presence, and power, and this is proper to him alone.
God's omnipresence cannot be demonstrated from omnipotence or divine action; it is held by faith and authority.
Agents can act immediately on what they are not present to.
God has no real relation to place, and his new presence implies no change in him.

qrdBas-d1e4896.summary: The combined distinctions 43-44 of Book 2 are represented by a single, textually fragmentary item: folios 167v-168r are missing from the witness and a further break occurs at 169r. What survives treats three topics. It concludes a discussion of interior sin close to d42: thought is in the will's power, so sin can occur by morose delectation, the will is a partial cause of the mental word, and sin is divided five ways. It preserves a fragment on the sin against the Holy Spirit (d43), which is irremissible only in that it is rarely or never forgiven in fact. And it treats the power of sinning (d44) more fully: taken as the created will, that power is from God and good in its positive reality, God causes neither sin's deformity nor merely potential relations, and peccability is intrinsic to created but not to uncreated free choice. The item and the Book 2 commentary close with the 1516 printer's colophon. Any summary of these distinctions rests on this incomplete text.
claims: Sin can occur in thought alone, since thought is within the will's power.
The sin against the Holy Spirit is irremissible only in a qualified sense.
The power of sinning, as the created will, is from God and good; God does not cause sin's deformity.
Peccability belongs intrinsically to created free choice but not to free choice as such.

qrdBas-de49.summary: Partial summary of Book 1 of Bassolis's Sentences commentary, based only on the Prologue (eight questions) and distinction 37, which are 2 of the book's 50 direct divisions. The Praefatio and distinctions 1-36 and 38-48 are not covered. Within this subset, Book 1 opens with a full account of theology. Evident abstractive knowledge of God is possible to a wayfarer by divine power, while revealed doctrine is necessary for man's supernatural end. God under the formally distinct ratio of deity is theology's subject. Our theology is not science in the strict sense but an 'extended faith', an aggregate of habits independent of metaphysics, and it is practical, ordered to directing charitable love of God, whereas God's and the blessed's theology is speculative. In distinction 37 the treatment of God turns to omnipresence, which Bassolis holds by faith and authority alone, denying that it can be demonstrated from omnipotence. A recurring thread across both is his insistence on the limits of natural demonstration about God, together with the possibility of supernaturally given evident knowledge.
claims: Theology's subject is God under the ratio of deity; our theology is practical and not science in the strict sense.
Many truths about God, including omnipresence, are held by faith rather than demonstrated by natural reason.

qrdBas-de49z3.summary: Partial summary of Book 2 of Bassolis's Sentences commentary, based only on the final division, distinctions 43-44, which is 1 of the book's 37 direct divisions; the Praefatio and distinctions 1-42 are not covered. Even that division survives in a lacunose text. The covered material concerns the end of Book 2's treatment of sin: interior sin in thought and its divisions, the sin against the Holy Spirit as irremissible only in fact, and the power of sinning, which as the created will is from God and good, intrinsic to created free choice, while God is not the cause of sin's deformity. The book ends with the 1516 Paris printer's colophon.
claims: The created will, as the power of sinning, is from God and good in its positive reality.
The sin against the Holy Spirit is irremissible only in a qualified sense.

qrdBas.summary: Partial summary of John Bassolis's Commentary on the Sentences, based only on Books 1 and 2, which are 2 of the work's 4 books; Books 3 and 4 are not covered. Book 1 is covered only by its Prologue and distinction 37, and Book 2 only by distinctions 43-44. Within this narrow sample, the commentary appears as a Scotist-inflected but independent work. It engages Scotus, Aquinas, and Henry of Ghent closely, defining theology's subject as God under the formally distinct ratio of deity. It denies that our theology is science strictly speaking and holds it practical, ordered to charitable love of God, and it stresses the limits of natural demonstration (God's omnipresence is held by faith), while allowing supernaturally given evident knowledge. In moral theology it holds that the created will, as the power of sinning, is good and from God, and that God does not cause sin's deformity.
claims: Theology's subject is God under the ratio of deity; our theology is practical and not science strictly.
Natural reason cannot demonstrate many truths about God, such as omnipresence.
The created will, as the power of sinning, is from God and good; sin's deformity is not caused by God.
